description_full: McKesson Corporation provides healthcare services in the United States and internationally. It operates through four segments: North American Pharmaceutical, Oncology & Multispecialty, Prescription Technology Solutions, and Medical-Surgical Solutions. The company distributes branded, generic, specialty, biosimilar and over-the-counter pharmaceutical drugs, and other healthcare-related products; delivers products to retail pharmacies, hospitals, long-term care centers, clinics, and institutions; and provides logistics and distribution services for manufacturers. It also provides consulting, outsourcing, technological, and other services, as well as sells financial, operational, and clinical solutions to pharmacies; gene therapy with InspiroGene, practice consulting, and vaccine distribution services; and technology solutions, as well as research, insights, technologies, and services to improve cancer and specialty care. In addition, the company helps in solving medication access, affordability, and adherence challenges for patients by working across healthcare to connect patients, pharmacies, providers, pharmacy benefit managers, health plans, and biopharma companies. Further, it offers technology services, which includes electronic prior authorization, prescription price transparency, benefit insight, dispensing support services, patient enrollment, third-party logistics, and wholesale distribution support; medical-surgical supplies, laboratory equipment, pharmaceutical distribution, logistics, and other services to healthcare providers, including physician offices, surgery centers, hospital reference labs, nursing homes, hospice and home health care agencies, government facilities, and online marketplaces and retailers. McKesson Corporation was founded in 1833 and is headquartered in Irving, Texas.

financial_summary: McKesson Corporation is a large-cap healthcare business with a $127.3B market cap on $403.4B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +13% over the past three years and +8% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.

Returns on capital run at 5% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, and 5% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $5.7B in free cash flow — roughly 1 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.29× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.2× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 25× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield of 4.0% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and profit capture is only 0.2× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sector_headwinds.text: Low reinvestment-driven growth suggests the compounding engine has stalled
Fragmented industry with below-average profit capture — no moat to protect margins
Trading near 52-week highs — the market has already recognised the story
Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Insiders are net sellers (100% sell ratio, net $21.6M) — the people closest to the business are reducing their personal stake
Gross margin trails most Healthcare peers — competitors appear to have the pricing hand
Patent cliffs, drug-pricing reform, and reimbursement pressure — a single regulatory change can reset the pricing power that justifies the multiple.
Clinical trial concentration risk — binary FDA outcomes on a lead asset can wipe out billions in market cap in a single session.
GLP-1 disruption across sub-sectors — weight-loss drugs are reshaping demand for orthopaedics, cardiovascular devices, and sleep-apnea treatments in ways not yet priced in.

mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 14% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 2% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 32% and a beta of 0.42, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y -0.24 vs 5y 0.30), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $715.3M traded a day.

The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 73%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $1,041 to $1,754 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 26% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 4.5% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 4.7% (vs the 8% bar).
The 14 covering analysts target $1,144 on average, 4% above the price.
The price implies 4.6% annual cash-flow growth, 3pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 5% falls short of the cost of capital of 8.0%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 5.20).
It runs a 5% gross margin and converts 1% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.29x.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.2x net debt to EBITDA ($4.0B of cash against $5.3B of debt), with interest covered 25.1x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 6.3, in the safe zone).
The current ratio of 0.85 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 13.4% over 3 years, 11.1% over 5 years and 7.8% over 10 years, so growth is accelerating.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 6.9% a year over five years.
Capex runs 1.5x depreciation (0.1% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is 12, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.1%), and institutions hold 93%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (12 sales, net $21.6M sold).
It returns 4.0% a year to shareholders (3.7% in buybacks and 0.3% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 5.1% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 31 consecutive years, raising it 6.7% a year over the last five.
people: With about 41,600 employees, each generates about $9.7M of revenue, 25.7x the Healthcare median, and revenue has grown 8.0% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $137K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $7.0M (1x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
